A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same next-token versus MCQ evaluation study. Their text, equations, figures, tables and included appendices support reliable comparison despite the title change and extensive restructuring.

before.justification: v3 reports original LLM experiments, including accuracy and distributional results for dice, coins, preferences and choices in Section 4 and Appendices E–F, plus a medical case study.

after.justification: v4 reports original experiments comparing explicit and implicit probabilistic reasoning, including medical Statistics results in Figure 6 and discarded probability mass measurements in Table 2.

M1.justification: Both versions reformulate MCQs as text completion and examine probabilities assigned to possible outcomes. v4 renames the framework and explains softmax and multi-token probability computation more explicitly; these disclosures do not establish a changed core procedure.

E1.justification: The four original task families remain, and medical prevalence reasoning already appears in v3's case study. v4 extends this existing coverage through the Statistics dataset, including synthetic maternity and pediatric ward contexts alongside surgical wards (Appendix A.5).

E2.justification: Conventional MCQ answering remains the comparison method for next-token evaluation. No competing evaluation framework is added or removed. The changed LLM roster concerns the systems being evaluated rather than alternative evaluation baselines.

E3.justification: The evaluated panel changes from 13 to 10 models, removing examples such as Llama-4-Scout and QwQ-32B and adding Qwen3-30B-A3B and Qwen3-235B-A22B. v4 introduces 200 randomized medical prompts and revises stated totals for retained scenarios, including Dice from 3080 to 939. The counting conventions are not reconciled, so these totals do not establish equivalent reductions in actual evaluations.

E4.justification: v4 adds a check of probability assigned to unscored continuation tokens (Section 3.6, Table 2) and revises the medical and label-bias case studies. Distinct earlier analyses disappear, including biased Preference accuracy in v3 Figure 17 and detailed coin and choice distribution examples in Figures 11 and 13.

E5.justification: v3 reports binomial significance tests and significance stars in its accuracy figures. v4 removes these and adds error bars to accuracy plots; Figure 6 explicitly describes variance. The calculation of the new bars and any repeated-run or seed counts are not specified.

E6.justification: v4 adds Statistics accuracy and discarded-mass results, while v3's numerical Tables 7–18 disappear. Retained values also change: phi-4's reported probability of 'A' among six equiprobable choices changes from 0.82 in v3 Figure 6b to 0.43 in v4 Table 3. The medical example uses different inputs, so its MCQ likelihood changing from 89.9% to 99.96% is not a controlled performance gain.

T1.justification: The mathematical basis remains outcome probabilities and comparison with known distributions. No substantive theorem, proof or formal derivation is added or revised. The additional softmax and sequence-probability explanations document the retained procedure.

C1.justification: Both versions claim that successful MCQ answering can mask poor integration of probabilistic evidence into text generation, including biases and inappropriate responses to partial or irrelevant evidence. The renamed framework and additional medical evidence preserve this central contribution.

C2.justification: v4 drops the cognitive-dissonance analogy and qualifies belief as a possible interpretation of token probabilities. It adds substantive discussion of temperature effects and explicitly limits scoring to relative probabilities among accepted outcomes. The original caveats about prompt wording and distribution coverage remain.

D1.justification: v4 explicitly describes multi-token probability handling, unquantized precision, and Statistics generation ranges and prompts. v3's approximately six-day evaluation time and table of exact parameter counts are omitted. Prompt templates and parameter ranges for the original four task families remain available.

R1.justification: v4 expands discussion of probabilistic reasoning with Nafar et al. (2025), Feng et al. (2025) and Paruchuri et al. (2024), while removing cognitive-dissonance and philosophical credence references. Its central positioning relative to Hu and Levy and Qiu et al. remains.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, and Revealed Belief/Stated Answer terminology is replaced throughout. Related work moves from Section 5 to Section 2, methodology is reorganized, and the separate scenario-description and prompt-example appendices are combined in v4 Appendix A.

P2.justification: Figures are substantially reorganized: v3 Figure 4 becomes v4 Figures 4–5, while v3 Figure 6 becomes v4 Figure 7 and Table 3. v4 adds Table 2 and Figure 6, redraws label-bias panels, removes numerous appendix displays, and adopts a different journal layout and chart styling.

improvement.justification: v4 strengthens methodological scrutiny through the discarded-mass check and supports the medical example with 200 randomized prompts. However, it removes detailed numerical appendices, including L1 and KL results for metrics still named in Section 3.4, and significance analyses. Unexplained changes in reported counts and retained scores also reduce traceability. These substantive gains and losses prevent a reliable net judgment of overall improvement.
